Native
NAY-tiv
a. (belonging to a person by birth; pertaining to the place of one's birth)
Latin nativus, from natus, born, the past participle of nasci, to be born. A native land is, at root, simply the land a man was born into, before any choice of his own entered the matter.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah's oracle against Shallum, the son of Josiah who reigned briefly as Jehoahaz before being carried captive to Egypt, gives the word its one appearance in the Authorized Version, and does so with unusual finality: Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country. The dead, meaning Josiah, is not the one to mourn; the living exile, carried off from the land of his birth with no promise of ever seeing it again, is the greater grief. Jeremiah reverses the natural instinct to weep hardest for the grave and directs it instead toward the harder fate of permanent exile from one's native ground.

The weight the prophecy places on never seeing one's native country again only makes sense against the whole Old Testament's assumption that the land itself was bound up with covenant identity — not merely a birthplace in the modern, sentimental sense, but the specific inheritance promised to the fathers. To be exiled forever from it was not simply homesickness; it was a living picture of covenant curse, the same threat rehearsed throughout Deuteronomy's warnings, now falling on one particular king by name. Shallum's native country was never his by mere accident of birth in Israel's own theology; it was covenant ground, and losing it forever was the specific and severe judgment Jeremiah is here commanded to announce.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): pertaining to the place or country of one's birth; also, born in a particular place or country.

expand to see more

NATIVE, a. Belonging to one by birth; pertaining to the place or country where a person was born.

EXILE, n. Banishment; enforced removal from one's native country; also, the person so banished.

OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or promise, invoking God as a witness to the truth of what is declared.

INHERITANCE, n. That which is or may be inherited; a possession received by right of birth or covenant.

CAPTIVE, n. One taken prisoner, especially in war; one held in bondage or servitude.

Key Scripture

Jer 22:10 — "Weep ye not for the dead, neither bemoan him: but weep sore for him that goeth away: for he shall return no more, nor see his native country."

Jer 22:11 — "For thus saith the LORD touching Shallum the son of Josiah king of Judah, which reigned instead of Josiah his father, which went forth out of this place; He shall not return thither any more:"

Psa 137:1 — "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion."

Deu 28:36 — "The LORD shall bring thee, and thy king which thou shalt set over thee, unto a nation which neither thou nor thy fathers have known; and there shalt thou serve other gods, wood and stone."

Modern Corruption

Native land is flattened into a sentimental attachment to a birthplace, when Jeremiah's oracle and the covenant curses behind it treat exile from native ground as the visible enactment of a broken covenant, not homesickness.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself; native still names what belongs to a person by birth. The principle worth recovering is why Jeremiah treats Shallum's permanent exile as a heavier grief than his father's death. In the Old Testament's own frame, the land of Israel was never merely a native country in the generic modern sense but a specific covenant inheritance, sworn to the fathers and held on the condition of obedience.

Psalm 137's weeping by the rivers of Babylon is the same grief given voice from the exiles' own side, and Deuteronomy's earlier curse names the mechanism behind it in advance: covenant unfaithfulness would end in exile to a nation Israel had never known. Shallum's lost native country is therefore not a private sorrow of displacement but a public, prophetic sign that the covenant curses were no longer merely threatened but had begun to fall.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew moledet (H4138), kindred, native land, birthplace; the noun behind “native country” in Jeremiah 22:10, from yalad, to bear or beget.

expand to see more

Hebrew moledet (H4138) — kindred, native land, birthplace; the word rendered “native country” in Jeremiah 22:10, the same used of Abraham's own homeland in Genesis 12:1.

Hebrew erets (H776) — land, earth, country; the general noun paired with moledet in this construction.

Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to go into exile; the standing Old Testament verb for the captivity this oracle foretells.

Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to return, to turn back; explicitly and permanently denied Shallum, he shall return no more.

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; the covenant category the native land belonged to, deeper than mere birthplace.

Usage

"“he shall return no more, nor see his native country” — Jeremiah's oracle over Shallum's exile."

"“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept” — the same exile's grief from within."

"“The LORD shall bring thee... unto a nation which thou hast not known” — the covenant curse that made such exile possible."
